key_findings.finding: At4g32460 is BIIDXI/BDX (also reported as BIDXII in the seed-endosperm paper), a DUF642 cell-wall protein. The strongest primary evidence is PMID 25442819: At4g32460 and At5g11420 proteins had previously been shown to interact in vitro with the catalytic domain of AtPME3/At3g14310; BIIDXI/At5g11420 overexpression increased total PME activity during germination and improved germination, whereas At4g32460 antisense and two SALK lines reduced leaf PME activity and produced very short, seedless siliques. This supports regulation of PME activity and developmental phenotypes, but the interaction assay was in vitro and the study did not establish a direct catalytic mechanism or prove AtPME3 is the in-vivo substrate/partner.

source_tools.relevance: Primary paper abstract and full-text preview with interaction, gain/loss-of-function, PME activity, germination and siliques
Independent search result confirming the same primary-study findings

key_findings.finding: BIIDXI expression/localization is developmentally and tissue regulated: PMID 25442819 reports promoter-reporter expression in imbibed embryos, vascular tissues of primary/lateral roots, leaves, stems, stamens and petals; PMID 29238286 reports auxin induction and increased cell-wall localization of BIIDXI during early Meloidogyne incognita inoculation. These observations establish expression and localization correlations, not by themselves direct PME regulation.

source_tools.relevance: Primary 2014 paper full-text preview for tissue expression
Primary 2017 paper abstract for auxin induction and induced cell-wall localization during nematode inoculation

key_findings.finding: For seed/endosperm development, PMID 29137987 found bdx-1 mutants with misshapen embryos and an altered homogalacturonan methyl-esterification pattern: unesterified homogalacturonans were scarce in bdx-1 endosperm during embryo bending and in mature seeds. This links BIIDXI genetically to pectin methyl-esterification status and embryo morphology, but is associative with respect to PME enzyme activity and does not identify a specific PME or direct molecular mechanism.

For hypocotyl/root-shoot growth, PMID 30253266 showed that bdx-1 seedlings had longer hypocotyls, BIIDXI overexpressors were auxin resistant, bdx-1 hypocotyl epidermal cells accumulated auxin, and PIN1 distribution differed; the authors concluded BIIDXI affects hypocotyl elongation through auxin efflux. PME/pectin methyl-esterification is contextual background in the abstract, so this is mechanistic evidence for an auxin-flux developmental pathway but not direct evidence that BIIDXI changes PME activity in that experiment.

For stress-related development, PMID 36432778 found heat-induced BIIDXI expression changes, reduced thermotolerance in bdx-1 seedlings, and thermopriming-associated PME activity increases in WT but not bdx-1. This supports BIIDXI-dependent PME activation in thermopriming/thermotolerance, but the evidence remains genetic/physiological rather than a demonstrated direct biochemical activation mechanism.
